extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors; corporate communicators; organizational leaders and practitioners of publicity/PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and standards for the practice of public relations counsel: how to analyze publics, select methods and media, plan and execute campaigns, and the ethical obligations of PR practitioners. Emphasizes strategy, audience segmentation, use of mediums, events, third-party validation, and refusal of harmful work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret client to the public and public to the client
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel 'directs and supervises the activities of his clients wherever they impinge upon the daily life of the public. He interprets the client to the public, which he is enabled to do in part because he interprets the public to the client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice should be given on all occasions the client appears before the public (concrete acts or ideas). The counsel's role includes diagnosing how the client will be perceived and advising changes in conduct, presentation, or message to align client image with public expectations (examples throughout the book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select among the printed, spoken and visualized word — advertising, lectures, the stage, the pulpit, the newspaper, the photograph, the wireless, the mail, or any other form of thought communication — according to where the target public obtains information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide positive, verifiable evidence rather than mere denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere denial of a rumor accomplishes little; the counsel must give the public positive evidence of the client's intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to counter a rumor of a hotel's impending closing, counsel recommended immediately renewing the maître d'hôtel's long-term contract and publicizing it so that the public would see concrete evidence the hotel intended to remain in business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplify existing content through third-party validation and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Make existing valuable editorial or other content 'felt and appreciated' by wider or different publics without altering the original content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a magazine's article was turned into an inquiry among influential men; the collated abstract was furnished gratuitously to newspapers and journals, reprinted by organizations, and used as the basis for addresses abroad — increasing the magazine's prestige without changing its content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure endorsements and recognitions from respected authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain letters, commendations, or uses of material by respected public figures to increase credibility and reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Herbert Hoover's commendation and distribution of an article led relief committees to use the piece and raised the magazine's influence; endorsements function as authoritative third-party validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scientific/expert authority to substantiate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ physicians, scientists, or recognized experts to make a truth articulate and persuasive to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commissioning a physician's survey to promote bacon as a sound breakfast increased consumption; founding a national radium bank to create an impression about availability of radium for cancer treatment. Research or expert studies should be used as the basis for public education and news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target opinion leaders and group leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate ideas to group leaders whose espousal will influence the larger group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: persuading leading club women to express preference for long hair helped modify the bobbed-hair vogue; identify and enlist leaders who reflect and shape the attitudes of their groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment publics and tailor messages to each audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide material into categories based on the publics to which it will appeal and tailor content accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lithuania campaign: material was prepared separately for ethnologists, language students, sporting fans, jewelers, music lovers, senators, representatives, etc., with different messages and channels for each segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-channel, phased campaigns using every avenue of approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ mass meetings, petitions, lectures, mail, advertising, radio, motion pictures and other avenues in coordinated phases to capitalize public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel should plan campaigns that combine and sequence channels to build knowledge and action (e.g., Lithuania used meetings, petitions, congressional appeals, advertising, radio, motion pictures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create symbolic events and ceremonies to dramatize messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage inaugurations, launches, or ceremonies involving prominent figures that will symbolize and dramatize the client's intentions or messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: naming and launching a ship (Piave) with prominent Italian-Americans and sending images/messages to Italy to raise morale; having mayors send first radio messages at an inauguration. Symbolic acts are converted into news and moral signals by the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build coalitions and present non-partisan unity to unite disparate groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Form non-partisan committees and gather representatives from diverse groups to present a homogeneous public appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: forming a non-partisan committee for the League of Nations that united women from many affiliations to make a united appeal; coalition-building creates visible unity that leverages passive sympathies into active support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit interlapping group formations and shifting group affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interlocking and shifting memberships of groups in society to reach and change public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that people belong to many overlapping groups which change over time; craft appeals that move through these overlapping circles to diffuse ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify publics with granular lists and direct-by-mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify public into groups by geography, profession, business, religion, economic position, and preferences; use lists for targeted direct mail or communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct-by-mail campaigns are powerful when lists of individuals are available and correctly segmented by relevant criteria; the classification of publics is one of the counsel's most important functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the medium appropriate to the message and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to announce changes or messages by telegraph, circular, advertising, or other means depending on the client and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: different clients were advised differently — one to use telegraph, another circular, another advertising — selection depends on urgency, audience, and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the client's personality and practices part of the campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate the client's personal attributes, labor policies, hygienic factory aspects, or other genuine qualities into public-facing campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advising clients to publish books, found scholarships, or exhibit wares in schools/museums; authentic behaviors and policies can be leveraged to build goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert studies and treatises into newsworthy stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn historically-correct or academic treatises into interesting stories of news value to gain public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roumania example: rather than issuing dry treatises, the counsel advised making the studies into news stories which the public would read avidly — narrative and angle matter for news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research, surveys and collated responses as press material
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct inquiries or surveys among influential groups, collate and analyze answers, and furnish abstracts or results to press and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: creating inquiries based on magazine articles, using abstracts for free distribution to newspapers and class journals, and reprints by organizations to extend reach and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on publicity stunts; pursue substantive, sustained efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: While some may think PR is circus-agent stunts, the modern counsel must apply substantive analysis and sustained methods rather than ephemeral tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations show use of research, targeted messaging, events, and coalitions to produce durable change in opinion rather than one-off stunts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand public opinion as group/herd phenomena and plan accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is often the product of groups and herd behavior rather than individual, fully-informed judgments; counsel must take this psychological reality into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy should focus on how ideas get accepted by groups (competition of ideas in the 'market') and on using group processes (leaders, rituals, endorsements) to create acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make actions that have implicit meanings — dramatize realities to create impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public acts that carry desired implications (e.g., opening a post office as evidence of a community's desirability) instead of mere assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage local events in ways that attract national attention and let the public infer the intended qualities; concrete actions are persuasive because they are harder to dismiss than claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge campaign results and client acceptability from an ethical point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel 'must judge the results which his work would accomplish from an ethical point of view' and maintain scrutiny of actions to avoid propagating unsocial or harmful movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should refuse retainers or clients whose public campaigns would be morally objectionable or damaging to the larger society, even if legally defensible; maintain standards of integrity over partisan pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize counsel's social obligation to present facts and ideas of social utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The social value of the counsel lies in bringing to the public facts and ideas of social utility which would not otherwise gain acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR work should aim not only at private advantage but at circulating ideas that have genuine public benefit; the counsel plays a role in forming 'public conscience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing 'education' with 'propaganda' — be aware of point-of-view relativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The only difference between 'propaganda' and 'education' is point of view — advocacy of what we believe is education; advocacy of what we don't believe is propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of this relativity; because perception depends on viewpoint, counsel must be extra vigilant about methods and ethics to prevent their work being dismissed as dishonest or misleading.
